rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah’s central claim is the certainty of reward and punishment, and its oaths testify to that claim.
rows.anchor: the central theme of the sūrah is to substantiate reward and punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers evade arguments for resurrection by accusing the Prophet of being a poet or soothsayer inspired by jinn or devils; the oath refutes this allegation.
rows.anchor: They would allege that he is, God forbid, a poet or a soothsayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath invokes both the known and unknown worlds: history and observable places attest to judgment, while the unseen is intellectually recognized through God’s attributes and the fitting outcomes of deeds.
rows.anchor: Both the known and the unknown worlds bear witness to this

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah first substantiates reward and punishment through the histories of ancient nations, then through the unseen fates of the companions of the right and left hands.
rows.anchor: substantiated first by the historical account of certain ancient nations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The noble messenger who brought the revelation is Gabriel, whose nobility refutes the claim that a jinn or devil inspired it.
rows.anchor: The attribute “noble” is mentioned here to refute the claim cited above

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses restate positively what the preceding verses denied: people who wanted faith and valued the reminder would recognize that the Qur’an is neither poetry nor soothsaying.
rows.anchor: what has been stated a bove in a positive manner

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their evasions arise because they rarely desire faith or attentive benefit from the reminder; people lacking that desire look for excuses to avoid truth.
rows.anchor: seldom does the desire to embrace faith and to listen carefully and intently arises in them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verbs in the phrases about believing and remembering express intention, a customary use of verbs in Arabic.
rows.anchor: the verbs express intention, and it is very customary in Arabic for a verb to express intention

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh leaders could distinguish divine speech from poetry and soothsaying, but base desires buried their occasional impulse to acknowledge truth; the passage addresses the leaders, not the masses.
rows.anchor: the leaders of the Quraysh and not their masses which are referred to here

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A detailed rebuttal of calling the Qur’an poetry or soothsaying is given in Sūrah al-Shu‘arā’, where the author directs readers for further treatment.
rows.anchor: I have explained all its aspects there

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse states positively what the previous verses stated negatively; tanzīl entails gradual progression and thorough arrangement, including God’s protection of revelation from human and jinn devils.
rows.anchor: It encompasses gradual progression and thorough arrangement in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the Qur’an a revelation from the Lord of the worlds points to its exalted status and the grave consequences of denying it.
rows.anchor: point to the exaltedness of the Qur’ān as well as the evil consequences of its denial

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage answers the accusation that the Prophet invented revelation: God vigilantly guards His messengers, who cannot alter the message or falsely attribute it to Him without immediate seizure and death.
rows.anchor: who cannot dare make any changes in them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat also answers Quraysh’s demand for a different Qur’an or a change to it: no one could save the Prophet from God if he altered the revelation.
rows.anchor: This demand and the response to it is mentioned thus

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the usual rendering of bi-l-yamīn as “by his right hand,” translates it according to Arabic linguistic principles, and notes that al-Ṭabarī gives the same translation.
rows.anchor: Al-T @abarī’s translation is also the same

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word watīn means the life-vein, king-vein, or heart-vein; the image conveys that God holds human life in His grasp and can end it instantly.
rows.anchor: The implication is that God is very near man and his life-vein is in His grasp

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Addressing Quraysh, the verse asks who could save the Prophet from God; because aḥad has plural usage here, the plural ḥājizīn is grammatically proper, as also illustrated at 33:32.
rows.anchor: hence it is absolutely in accordance with the principles of Arabic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s special protection makes messengers infallible because they carry the law and must not set a wrong example; ordinary people may falsely attribute things to God and receive respite, but face the consequences in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: It is because the messengers are entrusted with the sharī‘ah that they are rendered as infallible by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is a reminder from which the God-fearing benefit; its rejection is the rejecters’ own deprivation, and the verse reassures the Prophet that others value it.
rows.anchor: The God-fearing benefit from its reminders and they are the sought after ones

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is a warning that God knows who denies the message, so the deniers should expect to meet their fate.
rows.anchor: those who are denying should remember that they are not hidden from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers will soon regret their denial and lament the misfortune it brought upon them.
rows.anchor: soon this will be regretted by them, and they will bemoan their misfortune

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised reward and punishment are certain, not baseless news; the sūrah closes by recalling the inevitability with which it began, a recurring structural mark of Qur’anic coherence.
rows.anchor: One can see that the sūrah ends on the note with which it began

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to glorify God assures the Prophet not to despair but to wait patiently; glorification builds strength, patience, and confidence in God’s power to make His words come true.
rows.anchor: This glorification will inculcate strength, patience and confidence in him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah al-Muṭaffifīn supplements al-Infiṭār, sharing its theme and elaborating the division of righteous and defiant people at its end.
rows.anchor: This sūrah  is a supplement to S ūrah al-Infi ṭār

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Infiṭār reasons from God’s attributes displayed in the human body, while this sūrah reasons from the moral nature God gave people.
rows.anchor: attributes of God that are prominent in man’s physical being

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human nature loves justice and good and dislikes injustice and evil; this moral distinction shows that the Creator differentiates the just from the unjust rather than treating them alike.
rows.anchor: by his very nature man likes justice and what is good

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People commit injustice when other motives overpower their nature, as shown by the dishonest trader who protests when others cheat him.
rows.anchor: the very person who is dishonest in weighing to others cries out with anguish if others are dishonest with him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since God is just and created people with a love of justice, He must establish a day to reward those who honor that nature and punish those who disregard it.
rows.anchor: it is essential that He bring forth a day in which He

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an repeatedly uses this reasoning for the Day of Judgement; the author points to his discussion of 75:14–15.
rows.anchor: readers can take a look at what I have written under the following verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–6 censure people who demand fair treatment while cheating others; their conduct shows they do not expect to be raised before their Lord for judgement.
rows.anchor: An expression of regret on people who want

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 7–17 describe the fate of those who deny reward and punishment and live in disobedience to God.
rows.anchor: A mention of the fate of the defiant who had denied reward and punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 18–28 describe the fate of the loyal, faithful, and God-fearing.
rows.anchor: A mention of the fate of those loyal to God who professed faith in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 29–36 reverse today’s mockery: believers will rejoice and laugh at disbelievers who had mocked them.
rows.anchor: today the disbelievers do not care about anyone except their own selves and are making fun of the believers

none: This segment contains only the sūrah text and its translation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening warning is not a neutral statement; it also conveys a curse and censure.
rows.anchor: This sentence is not merely a statement of fact; curse and censure are also concealed in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taṭfīf means giving short measure or weight.
rows.anchor: The word !ْ#ْﺗﻄﻔﻴﻒ refers to measuring and weighing less

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse contrasts people who insist on full measure from others with their own dishonesty toward others, exposing a moral inconsistency rather than merely naming a trading practice.
rows.anchor: a person is very sensitive and vigilant that others should weigh and measure correctly for him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Such a cheater knows justice requires the same honesty for both sides; he violates his own nature from selfishness, committing open and mean injustice.
rows.anchor: he in fact goes against his own nature purely being overwhelmed with selfishness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God placed in people a moral barometer that makes them dislike oppression and like justice; when they oppress, desire or emotion overwhelms their ability to keep balance, not their ability to recognize right and wrong.
rows.anchor: The real reason, as pointed out above, is because he is so overcome by some desire or emotion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thieves, murderers, and adulterers would not want the same harm done to their own households, and even impartially acknowledge that society should protect life, wealth, and integrity for everyone.
rows.anchor: Only those people should be members of a society who protect the life, wealth and integrity of others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This nature shows that people distinguish good from evil and expect different treatment; God must therefore judge righteous and wrongdoers, and the deniers resist because they wish to evade that outcome.
rows.anchor: An obvious corollary of this is that the Almighty

rows.speaker: exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes report that dishonest measuring among the Anṣār occasioned revelation of this verse.
rows.anchor: While explaining this verse, our exegetes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author challenges that report’s setting: the sūrah is Meccan, and dishonest trade was at least as plausible among the Meccan traders as among the agricultural Anṣār.
rows.anchor: this sūrah is Makkan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if the Anṣār had the practice, it was no more prevalent than among the Meccans, who were traders, while the Anṣār’s profession was agriculture; the verse’s main point is innate recognition of justice, which implies judgement and accountability.
rows.anchor: In fact, there was a much greater chance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question expresses wonder at disbelievers’ attitude: everyone should fear the great day attested by human nature, when people rise before the Creator and are judged and recompensed.
rows.anchor: These verses express wonder at the attitude adopted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase Lord of the worlds carries arguments for the majesty and necessity of the Day and its judgements, which the author has explained elsewhere.
rows.anchor: the majesty and need of such a day and the verdicts given therein

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic denial rebuts the notion that no judgement will come or that the deniers will be favored because of their creed and deities; righteous and wicked will instead be far apart, with records in ‘illiyyūn and sijjīn.
rows.anchor: East and the West are

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sijjīn is a Qur’anic term, not its literal meaning; the Qur’an itself explains such terms, as with ‘illiyyūn and tasnīm later in this sūrah.
rows.anchor: not in its literal meaning; it is used as a name

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question what sijjīn is creates awe and dread, warning that anyone whose name or deeds are recorded there is doomed.
rows.anchor: meant to express the awe and dread found in the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sijjīn is the written register preserving sinners’ deeds without error or uncertainty; it determines the category of Hell for each person, and its name derives from sijn, jail.
rows.anchor: The qualification that this record is preserved in writing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deniers should not infer from the absence of present accounting that no one will call them to account; when judgement arrives, they will be doomed.
rows.anchor: those who rejected it will be doomed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The record omits none of the sinners’ words or deeds and offers no escape from doom; 18:49 illustrates their shocked response to its completeness.
rows.anchor: neither were any of their words and deeds left out from their record

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only people lacking even a trace of justice and mercy deny judgement; human nature itself testifies to accountability, while hearts corrupted by usurpation and transgression cannot envision it.
rows.anchor: no person can dare deny this day who has even the slightest semblance of justice and mercy in him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: I‘tidā’ is taking others’ rights, while ithm is failing to discharge rights one owes; habitual violators seek excuses to avoid accountability and quiet their conscience.
rows.anchor: The former refers to a person who seizes the rights of others while the latter refers to a person who does not discharge the rights of others imposed on him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People evade a reality because accepting it harms their desires and habits, then invent even lame excuses; the author connects this to 75:14–15.
rows.anchor: by accepting it his own desires an d habits

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Instead of answering the Qur’an’s reasoning with reasoning, deniers stubbornly dismiss its verses as ancient tales.
rows.anchor: instead of responding to reasoning through reasoning, they only express stubbornness and obduracy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s āyāt are arguments for the Day of Judgement, found in surrounding verses and in accounts of nations destroyed for rejecting the Hereafter; deniers brush them off as old tales.
rows.anchor: These arguments are mentioned in the previous verses and also in the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The evidence for judgement is undeniable in the world within and around people, but the rust of their deeds blocks truth from their hearts.
rows.anchor: undeniable facts which are evidenced by the world around man and that within him as well by his intellect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about what they earned refers back to the rights-usurpation and dereliction described under 83:12; valuing nature and reason lets them benefit, while base desires let sin gradually rust and overwhelm their faculties.
rows.anchor: gradually the rust of his misdeeds begins to settle on these faculties

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being held away from God refutes the deniers’ hope of retaining their worldly status in the Hereafter: they lose His blessings, the vision of Him, and even the chance to plead with Him.
rows.anchor: held away from their Lord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating thumma emphasizes the announcement to humiliate the deniers, who will taste what they vehemently denied.
rows.anchor: shows that they would be told these things in an emphatic manner

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage rejects the idea that righteous and wrongdoers share one record: the righteous have their own record in ‘illiyyūn.
rows.anchor: just as there will be a specific register for the wrong-doers, there will a specific register for the righteous

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about ‘illiyyūn conveys its grandeur: it is an exalted register containing the righteous’ deeds.
rows.anchor: in this world: it is a register

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Illiyyūn is a technical term for a written record containing every detail and kept in the custody of exalted angels.
rows.anchor: and it is in the custody of exalted angels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, only the favored ones may witness the record, since it is for them and no one else has access; verse 28 identifies them.
rows.anchor: only they would be able to come and see it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The righteous recline on thrones in bliss, surrounded by blessings from every side.
rows.anchor: it refers to the fact that blessings will engulf the believers from all sides
